subtopics.title: Biofuels and their generations
subtopics.theory_md:
**Biofuels** are fuels made from **biomass**, so they are renewable and nearly carbon-neutral: the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ released on burning was recently fixed by photosynthesis. Fossil fuels add old carbon, and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is the main greenhouse gas.
- **1st generation:** food crops. Ethanol from sugarcane, corn; biodiesel from soybean, palm oil. Food vs fuel conflict.
- **2nd generation:** non-food lignocellulose (rice straw, bagasse, wood) and non-edible oil (*Jatropha*). Needs pretreatment and cellulase.
- **3rd generation:** algae (*Chlorella*). High yield, no farmland, captures $\mathrm{CO_2}$; costly harvesting.
- **4th generation:** genetically engineered algae or cyanobacteria with carbon capture.
subtopics.basics_md: A biofuel is a fuel grown rather than dug up. Plants take CO2 from the air as they grow and give it back when the fuel burns, so the loop is nearly closed. Generations are just a ladder of feedstocks: food crop, farm waste, algae, engineered microbe.
key_points: Biofuel = fuel from biomass; renewable, near carbon-neutral
1st generation: food crops, food vs fuel problem
2nd generation: lignocellulosic or non-edible feedstock, needs pretreatment
3rd generation: algae; 4th: genetically engineered organisms

questions.q: Classify biofuels into generations with feedstock, examples, one advantage and one limitation of each.
questions.model_answer_md:
| Generation | Feedstock | Examples | Advantage | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | Food crops: sugar, starch, edible oil | Ethanol from sugarcane, corn; biodiesel from soybean, palm | Simple, established technology | Food vs fuel; land and water use |
| 2nd | Lignocellulose, non-edible oil | Ethanol from rice straw, bagasse; Jatropha biodiesel | Uses waste, no food competition | Lignin pretreatment and cellulase are costly |
| 3rd | Algae | Algal biodiesel from *Chlorella*, *Botryococcus* | High yield per hectare, no arable land, absorbs $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | Harvesting and drying are expensive |
| 4th | Genetically engineered algae, cyanobacteria | Engineered strains that secrete fuel | High yield, carbon capture | Early stage, biosafety |
points: Four generations named in order with feedstock

subtopics.title: Bioethanol and biodiesel
subtopics.theory_md:
**Bioethanol:** yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*) ferments sugar anaerobically, then the ethanol is distilled and blended with petrol (India: E20).
$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2}$; 180 g glucose gives 92 g ethanol, so the theoretical yield is $92/180 = 0.511$ g per g. Starch and lignocellulose are first hydrolysed to glucose (amylase, cellulase).

**Biodiesel:** **transesterification** of triglyceride (vegetable oil, used oil) with **methanol** and NaOH or KOH catalyst at about 60 °C gives **FAME** (biodiesel) and **glycerol**. Glycerol settles out; the ester is washed.
subtopics.basics_md: Ethanol: yeast eat sugar and leave alcohol and gas. Biodiesel: oil is a fat with three long tails on glycerol; methanol swaps the glycerol for methyl groups, giving thinner liquid esters that a diesel engine can burn.
key_points: Bioethanol: yeast fermentation of glucose, then distillation
Equation $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2}$
Biodiesel: transesterification of oil with methanol, NaOH/KOH catalyst
Products FAME and glycerol (by-product)

questions.why: Yeast converts glucose to ethanol and $\mathrm{CO_2}$; Acetobacter makes acetic acid.

questions.q: How much ethanol can be obtained theoretically from 1000 kg of glucose? A plant achieves 90% of this. Find the mass and the volume of ethanol obtained (density 0.789 kg/L).
questions.model_answer_md:
$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2}$: 180 g glucose gives $2\times46 = 92$ g ethanol.

- Theoretical: $1000 \times 92/180 = 511$ kg
- At 90%: $0.90 \times 511 = 460$ kg
- Volume: $460/0.789 = 583$ L

questions.q: How is biodiesel produced? Write the reaction in words.
questions.model_answer_md:
- Feedstock: vegetable oil (soybean, palm), non-edible oil (*Jatropha*), used cooking oil, algal oil.
- **Transesterification:** triglyceride + 3 methanol, with NaOH or KOH catalyst at about 60 °C.
- Products: 3 **fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) = biodiesel** + **glycerol**.
- Glycerol settles and is separated; biodiesel is washed and dried; used neat (B100) or blended (B20).

questions.q: In biodiesel production, the by-product is
questions.why: Transesterification replaces glycerol by methyl groups, releasing glycerol.

subtopics.title: Biogas production
subtopics.theory_md:
**Biogas** is made by **anaerobic digestion** of cattle dung, sewage sludge or food waste: about 50-70% $\mathrm{CH_4}$, 30-40% $\mathrm{CO_2}$, traces of $\mathrm{H_2S}$.

Four stages: **hydrolysis** (polymers to sugars, amino acids), **acidogenesis** (fatty acids, alcohols), **acetogenesis** (acetate, $\mathrm{H_2}$), **methanogenesis** by methanogens (*Methanobacterium*): $\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightarrow CH_4 + CO_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2 + 4H_2 \rightarrow CH_4 + 2H_2O}$.

**Plant (floating gas-holder, KVIC):** inlet tank (dung + water 1:1), underground digester (30-37 °C), floating gas holder, gas outlet pipe, outlet for spent slurry used as manure.
subtopics.basics_md: Bacteria in a sealed tank without air chew waste in a relay: big molecules, then acids, then acetate, then methane. The gas collects under a floating drum that rises as it fills.
key_points: Anaerobic digestion of dung or organic waste by bacteria and methanogens
Four stages: hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, methanogenesis
Composition: CH4 50-70%, CO2 30-40%
Plant parts: inlet, digester, gas holder, gas outlet, slurry outlet (manure)

figures.caption: Methane, the fuel gas of biogas

questions.q: Explain the production of biogas. Describe a biogas plant with its parts.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Biogas** is a gas mixture (CH4 50-70%, CO2 30-40%, traces of H2S) produced by **anaerobic digestion** of cattle dung, sewage and organic waste.

**Stages**
1. Hydrolysis: carbohydrates, proteins, fats to sugars, amino acids, fatty acids
2. Acidogenesis: volatile fatty acids, alcohols, H2, CO2
3. Acetogenesis: acetic acid, H2, CO2
4. Methanogenesis: methanogens give $\mathrm{CH_4}$

**Plant (floating gas-holder type)**
- Inlet/mixing tank: dung and water 1:1 slurry
- Digester: underground tank at 30-37 °C
- Floating gas holder: rises as gas collects
- Gas outlet pipe to stove or lamp
- Outlet: spent slurry used as manure

**Benefits:** clean cooking fuel, sanitation, rich manure.
points: Labelled parts: inlet, digester, gas holder, gas pipe, slurry outlet

questions.why: Only methanogens form CH4, from acetate or from H2 + CO2.

subtopics.title: Definition, triad and process
subtopics.theory_md:
**Tissue engineering** (Langer and Vacanti) uses cells, scaffolds and signals to build biological substitutes that restore, maintain or improve tissue function.

**Triad:**
1. **Cells:** autologous or allogeneic; chondrocytes, keratinocytes, stem cells (MSCs, iPSCs).
2. **Scaffold:** 3D porous support that mimics the extracellular matrix (ECM).
3. **Growth factors (signals):** VEGF (vessels), BMP (bone), TGF-$\beta$.

**Process:** biopsy, isolate and expand cells, seed on scaffold, culture in a **bioreactor**, implant; scaffold degrades as tissue forms. Examples: skin for burns, cartilage, bladder. Main challenge: **vascularisation**. It is not gene therapy or cloning.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of building a wall: bricks are the cells, scaffolding holds them in shape, and the builder's instructions are the growth factors. Take the scaffolding away once the wall stands.
key_points: Definition: cells + scaffold + signals to restore tissue function
Triad: cells, scaffold, growth factors
Process: biopsy, expansion, seeding, bioreactor culture, implantation
Examples: skin, cartilage, bone; challenge vascularisation

points: B) Scaffolds, cells, and growth factors
The triad; enzymes alone or only genetic modification miss scaffold and cells

questions.q: Which growth factor mainly promotes blood vessel formation in engineered tissue?
questions.why: VEGF drives angiogenesis; BMP is for bone.

questions.q: What is tissue engineering? Explain its key components and the process.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Definition:** application of engineering and life-science principles to make biological substitutes that restore, maintain or improve tissue function.

**Components (triad)**
1. Cells: autologous (patient's own) or stem cells
2. Scaffold: porous, biodegradable ECM-like support
3. Growth factors: VEGF, BMP, TGF-$\beta$

**Process**
1. Biopsy and isolation of cells
2. Expansion in culture
3. Seeding on the scaffold
4. Maturation in a bioreactor with nutrients, $\mathrm{O_2}$, mechanical stimulus
5. Implantation; scaffold degrades as new tissue forms

**Applications:** skin (burns), cartilage, bone, bladder. **Challenge:** vascularisation of thick tissue.

options: A donor of the same species
A cell bank of cancer lines
questions.why: Autologous cells carry no rejection risk.

subtopics.title: Scaffolds: properties, materials, fabrication
subtopics.theory_md:
**Ideal scaffold:** biocompatible; **biodegradable** at a rate matched to new tissue, with harmless products; **porous with interconnected pores** (about 100-500 $\mu$m for bone) for cell migration and nutrient flow; mechanical strength matched to the tissue; surface that supports cell adhesion; sterilisable.

**Materials:** natural (collagen, gelatin, chitosan, alginate, silk, hyaluronic acid) are bioactive but weak; synthetic (PLA, PGA, PLGA, PCL) are strong, reproducible but bio-inert; ceramics (hydroxyapatite, $\beta$-TCP) for bone.

**Fabrication:** electrospinning (nanofibres), solvent casting with particulate leaching (pores), freeze-drying, gas foaming, 3D printing.
subtopics.basics_md: The scaffold is a temporary house for the cells. It must let them in, feed them, hold them up, and leave when the real tissue arrives.
key_points: Biocompatible and biodegradable at matched rate
Interconnected porosity for cells and nutrients
Mechanical properties like the tissue; supports adhesion
Natural (bioactive, weak) vs synthetic (strong, inert) materials
Fabrication: electrospinning, particulate leaching, freeze-drying, gas foaming, 3D printing

figures.caption: Glycolic acid (PLGA is a copolymer of these two)

questions.q: PLGA, widely used for scaffolds, is a
options: Synthetic biodegradable copolymer of lactic and glycolic acid
questions.why: PLGA degrades by hydrolysis to lactic and glycolic acids.

questions.q: Which is NOT a desirable property of a tissue-engineering scaffold?
options: Degradation rate matched to tissue growth
questions.why: Students pick permanent; most scaffolds must degrade as tissue forms.

questions.q: List the properties of an ideal scaffold for tissue engineering.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. **Biocompatible:** no toxic or immune reaction
2. **Biodegradable** at a rate matching new tissue, harmless products
3. **Highly porous, interconnected pores** (100-500 $\mu$m for bone) for cell migration, $\mathrm{O_2}$ and nutrient flow
4. **Mechanical strength** matched to the host tissue
5. **Surface chemistry** that allows cell adhesion and growth
6. Sterilisable and easy to fabricate

questions.q: Compare natural and synthetic scaffold materials, and name three fabrication methods with one feature each.
questions.model_answer_md:
| Property | Natural (collagen, chitosan, alginate, silk) | Synthetic (PLA, PGA, PLGA, PCL) |
|---|---|---|
| Bioactivity | High, cell-binding sites | Low, bio-inert |
| Strength | Weak | Strong, tunable |
| Reproducibility | Batch variation | High |
| Immunogenicity | Some risk | Low |
| Degradation | Enzymatic, fast | Hydrolytic, controlled |

**Fabrication**
- Electrospinning: nanofibre mats like ECM
- Solvent casting + particulate leaching: controlled pore size
- Freeze-drying or gas foaming: highly porous sponges

topics.topic: Artificial limbs, joints and body parts

subtopics.title: Biomaterials: requirements and classes
subtopics.theory_md:
A **biomaterial** is a material that interfaces with biological systems to treat, augment or replace tissue. A **prosthesis** replaces a part; an **orthosis** supports one.

**Requirements:** biocompatible (no toxic or immune reaction), corrosion and wear resistant, adequate strength and fatigue life, modulus close to bone, low friction, sterilisable; **osseointegration** (bonding to bone) for titanium implants.

**Classes:**
- Metals: **Ti-6Al-4V**, 316L stainless steel, Co-Cr alloy.
- Ceramics: alumina, zirconia, **hydroxyapatite**, bioglass.
- Polymers: **UHMWPE**, **PMMA** (bone cement, lens), silicone, PEEK, Dacron.
- Composites: carbon fibre limbs.
subtopics.basics_md: Body fluid is warm salty water that corrodes metal and attacks plastics, and a hip moves a million times a year. A biomaterial has to survive that without upsetting the body.
key_points: Biomaterial definition; prosthesis vs orthosis
Requirements: biocompatibility, corrosion/wear resistance, strength, fatigue life
Metals: Ti-6Al-4V, 316L steel, Co-Cr
Ceramics: alumina, zirconia, hydroxyapatite; polymers: UHMWPE, PMMA, silicone

figures.caption: Methyl methacrylate, monomer of PMMA bone cement

options: Supports or braces an existing body part
questions.why: Replacement is a prosthesis; support is an orthosis.

questions.model_answer_md:

**Classification**

| Metals | Ti-6Al-4V, 316L steel, Co-Cr | Hip stem, plates, screws |
| Ceramics | Alumina, zirconia, hydroxyapatite, bioglass | Femoral head, bone coating |

| Composites | Carbon fibre | Limbs |

**Required properties:** biocompatibility, corrosion and wear resistance, strength and fatigue life, modulus close to bone, low friction, sterilisability, osseointegration.

subtopics.title: Joint replacement and stress shielding
subtopics.theory_md:
**Total hip replacement** has three parts:
- **Femoral stem:** titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) or Co-Cr, fixed in the thigh bone.
- **Head (ball):** Co-Cr, alumina or zirconia for hardness and low wear.
- **Acetabular cup** with a **UHMWPE** liner, low friction.

Fixation: **PMMA bone cement**, or cementless porous or hydroxyapatite-coated press-fit for bone ingrowth.

**Stress shielding:** a stiff implant (steel $\approx$ 200 GPa, Ti $\approx$ 110 GPa vs bone $\approx$ 10-30 GPa) carries the load, so bone is under-loaded and resorbs (Wolff's law), loosening the implant. Reduce by using lower-modulus alloys (Ti), porous or composite stems.
subtopics.basics_md: Bone stays strong only if it is used. If a very stiff rod takes all the load, the bone round it is left idle and wastes away.
key_points: Hip: femoral stem (Ti/Co-Cr), head (Co-Cr/ceramic), cup with UHMWPE liner
Fixation: PMMA cement or porous/HA-coated press-fit
Stress shielding: stiff implant takes load, bone resorbs (Wolff's law)
Remedy: modulus close to bone, porous or composite stem

questions.q: The acetabular cup liner in a total hip replacement is usually
questions.why: UHMWPE gives low friction and wear against the metal or ceramic head.

questions.q: What is stress shielding? How can it be reduced?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Stress shielding:** when an implant is much stiffer than bone, it carries most of the load and the surrounding bone is under-stressed. By **Wolff's law** bone then resorbs, and the implant loosens.

**Reduction**
- Use low-modulus materials (Ti alloy rather than Co-Cr or steel)
- Porous or composite stems that match bone modulus
- Shorter stems and bioactive coatings
points: Definition: stiff implant carries load, bone under-loaded
Remedy: modulus matched, porous or composite stems

questions.q: Describe the design of a total hip replacement and the materials used.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Parts and materials**
1. Femoral stem: Ti-6Al-4V or Co-Cr; strong, corrosion resistant
2. Femoral head: Co-Cr, alumina or zirconia; hard, low wear
3. Acetabular cup: metal shell with **UHMWPE** liner; low friction

**Fixation**
- Cemented: PMMA bone cement
- Cementless: porous or hydroxyapatite coating for bone ingrowth (osseointegration)

**Issues:** wear debris, stress shielding, loosening; life about 15-20 years.

subtopics.title: Artificial limbs and other body parts
subtopics.theory_md:
**Limbs:** passive (cosmetic); **body-powered** (cables and shoulder harness); **myoelectric** (EMG signals from residual muscles drive motors); bionic (sensors, feedback).

**Jaipur Foot** (1968, Dr P.K. Sethi and Ram Chandra Sharma): low-cost rubber and wood foot, allows squatting, walking barefoot and on uneven ground.

**Other parts:** pacemaker (heart rhythm), heart valves (mechanical or bioprosthetic), stents, cochlear implant (hearing), intraocular lens (PMMA), dialyser (artificial kidney), dental implants (Ti), LVAD.
subtopics.basics_md: A limb replacement is judged by what the wearer can do: cheap and robust for villages, fast and controllable for athletes.
key_points: Limb types: passive, body-powered, myoelectric (EMG), bionic
Jaipur Foot: 1968, low cost, rubber, squatting and barefoot walking
Other parts: pacemaker, valves, stents, cochlear implant, IOL, dialyser

subtopics.title: Bioprinting steps, techniques and uses
subtopics.theory_md:
**3D bioprinting** deposits a **bioink** layer by layer from a digital model to build tissue-like structures.

**Steps:** (1) **Pre-printing:** CT or MRI, CAD model, slicing, cell expansion, bioink. (2) **Printing.** (3) **Post-printing:** cross-linking, then **maturation in a bioreactor**.

**Techniques:** **extrusion** (high viscosity, high cell density; low resolution, shear stress); **inkjet** (fast, cheap, low viscosity); **laser-assisted** (nozzle-free, high resolution, costly); **stereolithography/DLP** (light, high resolution).

**Regenerative use:** skin for burns (even in situ), cartilage, bone, vessels, patient-specific implants with own cells, and disease models for drug testing. Whole organs remain a goal.
subtopics.basics_md: A bioprinter is an ordinary 3D printer whose ink is living cells in jelly, so it must be sterile, gentle and followed by time for the cells to grow into real tissue.
key_points: Three stages: pre-bioprinting, bioprinting, post-bioprinting (cross-linking, bioreactor)
Techniques: extrusion, inkjet, laser-assisted, SLA/DLP with trade-offs
Uses: skin, cartilage, bone, vessels, patient-specific implants, drug-testing models
Challenge: vascularisation; whole organs still research

questions.q: Which technique suits high-viscosity bioinks with high cell density?
questions.why: Extrusion pushes viscous ink through a nozzle; inkjet needs low viscosity.

questions.q: What is 3D bioprinting? Explain the steps and compare the main techniques.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Bioprinting:** layer-by-layer deposition of cell-laden bioink from a digital model to fabricate tissue constructs.

**Steps**
1. Pre-bioprinting: CT/MRI, CAD, slicing, cells and bioink prepared
2. Bioprinting: deposition of layers
3. Post-bioprinting: cross-linking and maturation in a bioreactor

| Technique | Ink | Merit | Demerit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extrusion | High viscosity | High cell density | Low resolution, shear stress |
| Inkjet | Low viscosity | Fast, cheap, viable | Clogging, low density |
| Laser-assisted | Wide range | Nozzle-free, high resolution | Costly |
| SLA/DLP | Photocurable | High resolution and speed | Needs light-safe cells |

questions.q: Which is the real reason a printed construct is not implanted straight away?
options: Cells must mature in a bioreactor to form functional tissue
questions.why: Students forget maturation; the printed shape is not yet functional tissue.

points: Definition: layer-by-layer bioink deposition from CT/MRI based CAD model
Patient-specific implants with own cells reduce rejection and donor shortage
Vascularised tissue; disease models and drug testing
Process: imaging, CAD, bioink, print, cross-link, bioreactor maturation

subtopics.title: Bioinks: properties, natural vs synthetic
subtopics.theory_md:
A **bioink** is living cells suspended in a biomaterial carrier (usually a hydrogel), often with growth factors.

**Ideal bioink:** **printability** (shear-thinning, then recovers; shape fidelity); fast **cross-linking** (alginate + $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, GelMA + UV, gelatin by cooling); biocompatibility and cell viability; bioactivity (RGD sites); mechanical strength; controlled biodegradation; porosity for $\mathrm{O_2}$ and nutrients.

**Natural hydrogels** (alginate, gelatin, collagen, fibrin, hyaluronic acid): bioactive, but weak and variable. **Synthetic** (PEG, Pluronic F127, PVA): strong, reproducible, bio-inert. Best: **hybrids** such as GelMA or alginate with a PCL frame.

**Challenges:** vascularisation, viability under shear, maturation time.
subtopics.basics_md: The ink has two jobs that pull against each other: be soft enough for cells to live in, and firm enough to hold its shape after printing.
key_points: Bioink = cells + hydrogel carrier (+ growth factors)
Shear-thinning, shape fidelity, fast cross-linking
Biocompatible, bioactive, biodegradable, porous
Natural: bioactive but weak; synthetic: strong but inert; hybrid is best

questions.q: Alginate bioink is commonly cross-linked by
questions.why: Ionic gelation: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ bridges the alginate chains.

questions.q: Shear-thinning of a bioink means its viscosity
options: Rises when pushed through the nozzle
Falls under shear and recovers after deposition
questions.why: It flows in the nozzle then regains stiffness to hold shape.

questions.q: What is a bioink? List the properties of a good bioink.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Bioink:** living cells in a printable biomaterial (hydrogel), with growth factors if needed.

**Properties**
1. Printability: shear-thinning, shape fidelity
2. Rapid cross-linking without harming cells
3. Biocompatibility, high cell viability
4. Bioactivity: cell adhesion sites (RGD)
5. Adequate mechanical strength
6. Controlled biodegradability
7. Porosity for nutrient diffusion

points: Bioink: cells in biomaterial carrier (hydrogel); biomaterial ink is without cells
Characteristics: printability and shear-thinning, rapid cross-linking, biocompatibility and viability, bioactivity (RGD), strength, controlled biodegradability, porosity
Comparison table: natural is bioactive, weak, variable; synthetic is strong, reproducible, bio-inert
Evaluation: natural more suitable for functional tissue because cells need bioactivity
Conclusion: hybrid or modified natural (GelMA, alginate-gelatin, PCL frame)

subtopics.title: Bioremediation: in situ, ex situ, phytoremediation
subtopics.theory_md:
**Bioremediation** uses living organisms, mainly microbes (also plants, fungi), to degrade, transform or immobilise pollutants (oil, pesticides, dyes, metals).

**In situ** (at the site, no excavation): **biostimulation** (add N, P, $\mathrm{O_2}$ for native microbes), **bioaugmentation** (add specialised microbes), bioventing, biosparging. Cheap; slow, less control.

**Ex situ** (soil excavated or water pumped): **landfarming, biopiles, composting, slurry-phase bioreactor**. Faster and controllable; costly.

**Phytoremediation:** phytoextraction (*Brassica juncea* absorbs metals), phytostabilisation, rhizofiltration, phytovolatilisation, rhizodegradation. Metals are not destroyed, only removed or immobilised.

Example: *Pseudomonas putida* superbug (Chakrabarty) for oil.
subtopics.basics_md: Clean the spill where it lies using the microbes already there, or dig it up and treat it in a controlled heap. Plants can also be used as living pumps for metals.
key_points: Definition: living organisms degrade or immobilise pollutants
In situ: biostimulation, bioaugmentation, bioventing, biosparging
Ex situ: landfarming, biopiles, composting, slurry bioreactor
Phytoremediation types; metals accumulated, not degraded

points: Bacteria and fungi (and plants) degrade or immobilise pollutants; robots, radiation and pressure are physical
In situ: treated at the site, no excavation; ex situ: removed and treated elsewhere
In situ cheaper and less disturbing; ex situ costlier
Ex situ better control and faster; in situ slower
Examples: bioventing, biostimulation vs landfarming, biopiles

questions.q: Adding N and P fertiliser to an oil-polluted beach so native bacteria grow faster is
questions.why: Biostimulation feeds native microbes; bioaugmentation adds new ones.

questions.q: What is phytoremediation? Name three types with an example.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Phytoremediation:** use of plants to clean polluted soil or water.
- **Phytoextraction:** roots take metals into shoots, e.g. Indian mustard (*Brassica juncea*)
- **Phytostabilisation:** plants immobilise pollutants in roots or soil
- **Rhizofiltration:** roots filter metals from water
- **Phytovolatilisation:** pollutant converted to a volatile form (Se, Hg)

Metals are removed or stabilised, not degraded.

questions.q: Landfarming is classed as
options: In situ, because soil stays on the land
Ex situ, because soil is excavated and spread
questions.why: Students call it in situ; the soil is dug up and treated.

subtopics.title: Aerobic and anaerobic, and bioremediation vs physicochemical
subtopics.theory_md:
**Aerobic:** $\mathrm{O_2}$ is the electron acceptor; end products $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, biomass; faster, best for petroleum hydrocarbons; needs aeration (activated sludge, bioventing).

**Anaerobic:** no $\mathrm{O_2}$; acceptors $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$; products $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ (biogas); slower; best for chlorinated solvents and sludge.

**Bioremediation vs physicochemical** (incineration, chemical oxidation, soil washing): bioremediation is cheap, low-energy, eco-friendly and slow, mainly for biodegradable organics; physicochemical is fast, costly, may leave secondary waste, handles high concentrations.
subtopics.basics_md: Same job, two styles: living cleaners that are slow, gentle and cheap, or machines and chemicals that are fast, harsh and expensive. Oxygen decides which microbes can work.
key_points: Aerobic: O2 acceptor, CO2 + H2O, faster; anaerobic: no O2, CH4/H2S, slower

subtopics.title: Biomining and the sustainability note
subtopics.theory_md:
**Biomining (bioleaching):** acidophilic bacteria *Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans*, *A. thiooxidans* and *Leptospirillum* (pH 1.5-3) extract Cu, U, Zn, Au from low-grade ore.

$\mathrm{4Fe^{2+} + O_2 + 4H^+ \rightarrow 4Fe^{3+} + 2H_2O}$
$\mathrm{CuS + 2Fe^{3+} \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2Fe^{2+} + S}$
$\mathrm{2S + 3O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2H_2SO_4}$

Metal is recovered from the leachate by cementation or electrowinning. Methods: heap, dump, tank. Merits: low cost, low-grade ore, less $\mathrm{SO_2}$ than smelting; in gold ore bacteria break the sulphide matrix.

**Sustainability link:** bioremediation + bioleaching + biofuels + biodegradable polymers (PLA, PHB) + biosensors.
subtopics.basics_md: Some bacteria live on iron and sulphur. Their waste, ferric iron and acid, dissolves the metal out of rock, so we get copper without smelting.
key_points: Organisms: Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans, A. thiooxidans, Leptospirillum
Bacteria oxidise Fe2+ to Fe3+ and S to H2SO4; Fe3+ dissolves metal sulphide
Recovery by cementation or electrowinning; heap, dump, tank leaching
Advantages: low cost, low-grade ore, less SO2

subtopics.title: Wastewater treatment, BOD and urban waste
subtopics.theory_md:
**Sewage treatment:** primary (settling), **secondary** (aerobic **activated sludge**, trickling filter: flocs of bacteria and protozoa oxidise organics, lowering **BOD**), then **anaerobic sludge digestion** to biogas. Also nitrification-denitrification ($\mathrm{NH_4^+ \rightarrow NO_3^- \rightarrow N_2}$) and constructed wetlands.

**BOD** = oxygen used by microbes in 5 days at 20 °C. High BOD means more organic pollution.
$$BOD_5 = (DO_i - DO_f)\times \frac{\text{bottle volume}}{\text{sample volume}}$$

**Urban waste:** segregate, anaerobic digestion (biogas to bio-CNG), composting, PETase for PET, PHA bioplastic from fatty acids.
subtopics.basics_md: Microbes eat the sewage's food and use up oxygen doing it. The more oxygen they use, the dirtier the water was.
key_points: Primary, secondary (activated sludge, flocs, BOD), sludge digestion to biogas
BOD = O2 used in 5 days; high BOD means more pollution
BOD5 = (DOi - DOf) x dilution factor
Urban waste: segregation, anaerobic digestion, composting, enzymes for plastics, PHA

questions.why: Microbes consumed more oxygen because more organic matter was present.

questions.q: 6 mL of wastewater is diluted to 300 mL. Initial DO is 8.5 mg/L and the DO after 5 days is 4.5 mg/L. Calculate $BOD_5$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Dilution factor $= 300/6 = 50$

Oxygen drop $= 8.5 - 4.5 = 4.0$ mg/L

$BOD_5 = 4.0 \times 50 = 200$ mg/L

subtopics.title: Industrial enzymes and denaturation
subtopics.theory_md:
Enzymes are specific biocatalysts that work at mild temperature and pH.
- **Amylase:** starch liquefaction, desizing, detergents
- **Protease:** detergents, leather dehairing
- **Lipase:** detergents, dairy flavour
- **Cellulase:** biofuel, denim stone-washing
- **Pectinase + protease:** fruit juice clarification
- **Rennet/chymosin:** cheese
- **Glucose isomerase:** high-fructose syrup; **streptokinase:** clot buster

**Denaturation** (heat, extreme pH, solvents, heavy metals, urea) breaks H bonds, ionic and hydrophobic interactions and S-S bridges; shape of active site is lost, activity falls. Primary structure stays intact.

**Michaelis-Menten:** $v = \dfrac{V_{max}[S]}{K_m + [S]}$; at $[S]=K_m$, $v = V_{max}/2$.
subtopics.basics_md: An enzyme works like a key in a lock, and heat or acid bends the lock. Industry uses that: boil it to kill spoilage enzymes, or choose heat-stable enzymes where heat is needed.
key_points: Enzyme-application pairs: amylase, protease, lipase, cellulase, pectinase, rennet
Denaturation: loss of 3D shape of active site, peptide bonds intact
Causes: heat, pH, solvents, heavy metals, urea
v = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]); v = Vmax/2 when [S] = Km

questions.q: An enzyme has $K_m = 2$ mM and $V_{max} = 50\ \mu$mol/min. Find the rate at $[S] = 2$ mM and 8 mM.
questions.model_answer_md:
$v = \dfrac{V_{max}[S]}{K_m+[S]}$

- $[S]=2$ mM: $v = \dfrac{50\times2}{2+2} = 25\ \mu$mol/min, which is $V_{max}/2$
- $[S]=8$ mM: $v = \dfrac{50\times8}{2+8} = 40\ \mu$mol/min

points: Activity depends on 3D shape of active site
Denaturation breaks H bonds, ionic, hydrophobic, S-S; primary structure intact; substrate cannot bind, activity lost
Industrial control: pasteurisation, thermostable enzymes (Taq, amylase), immobilisation, cold chain

subtopics.title: Microbial products and immobilised enzymes
subtopics.theory_md:
**Organic acids:** citric acid, *Aspergillus niger*; acetic acid, *Acetobacter aceti*; butyric acid, *Clostridium butylicum*; lactic acid, *Lactobacillus*.
**Ethanol:** *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*.
**Drugs:** penicillin, *Penicillium notatum*; **cyclosporin A**, *Trichoderma polysporum* (immunosuppressant); **statins**, *Monascus purpureus* (cholesterol). 
**Biopolymers:** PHA/PHB bioplastic.

**Immobilised enzymes** are fixed on a support by adsorption, entrapment, covalent binding or cross-linking. Advantages: reuse, better stability, easy product separation, continuous operation.

Fermentation: batch, fed-batch, continuous in a stirred-tank bioreactor.
subtopics.basics_md: Name the microbe, name the product. Immobilising an enzyme is like gluing it to beads so it can be fished out and reused.
key_points: Citric acid: A. niger; acetic: Acetobacter aceti; butyric: C. butylicum; lactic: Lactobacillus
Penicillin: Penicillium notatum; cyclosporin A: Trichoderma polysporum; statins: Monascus purpureus
Immobilisation: adsorption, entrapment, covalent, cross-linking
Advantages: reuse, stability, easy separation

questions.q: What are immobilised enzymes? Give methods and advantages.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Immobilised enzymes:** enzymes fixed on or in an insoluble support.

**Methods:** adsorption, entrapment in gel, covalent binding, cross-linking.

**Advantages:** reusable, more stable to heat and pH, easy separation of product, continuous operation.

subtopics.title: Role of biotechnology: economy, health, environment
subtopics.theory_md:
**Biotechnology** uses living organisms, cells or enzymes to make products and services.

- **Health:** recombinant insulin, hepatitis B and mRNA vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, PCR/ELISA/biosensors, gene and cell therapy.
- **Food security:** Bt cotton, Golden Rice, tissue culture, biofertilisers (*Rhizobium*), biopesticide (*Bacillus thuringiensis*).
- **Energy:** bioethanol, biodiesel, biogas.
- **Environment:** bioremediation, phytoremediation, wastewater treatment, biodegradable plastics (PLA, PHB).
- **Industry/economy:** enzymes, organic acids, antibiotics, jobs, exports, bioeconomy.

It links public health with sustainability: cleaner processes, less fossil fuel, safer food.
